title: Effects of Morning Strength and Power Priming Exercises on Afternoon Physical and Cognitive Performance in Male Rugby Union Players.
abstract: The objective of this study was to assess the effect of morning strength and power priming exercises on afternoon physical and cognitive performance in male rugby union players. On two occasions in a randomised, counterbalanced design, 25 male rugby union players completed morning physical (countermovement jump, 40 m linear sprint) and cognitive (rapid visual information processing; spatial working memory; paired associates of learning) assessments. Control (passive rest) or intervention (barbell back squat, 3 × 3 repetitions at 85% of one repetition maximum and barbell squat jump, 5 × 3 repetitions at 40% one repetition maximum) trials were implemented 5.5 h before afternoon assessments. Differences between morning and afternoon assessments were found in sprinting performance following intervention for 30 m fly (-0.08 ± 0.13 s, p = 0.004, ES: 0.615) and 40 m (-0.12 ± 0.17 s, p = 0.001, ES: 0.711) relative to control (0.03 ± 0.07 s, p = 0.022, ES: -0.476; 0.01 ± 0.09 s, p = 0.740, ES: -0.065, 30 m fly and 40 m, respectively). Afternoon countermovement jump flight time improved following intervention compared with control (2% vs. 0%, p = 0.012, ES: -0.53). No changes were found for cognitive assessments (p > 0.05). Morning strength and power priming exercises combining heavy-load traditional and light-load ballistic exercises effectively enhanced vertical jump and sprint performance, but not cognitive performance, in the afternoon in male rugby union players.

title: Influence of ballistic and conventional resistance training on bone properties in postmenopausal women: A randomised controlled trial.
abstract: High-load conventional resistance training (CRT) is recommended for osteoporosis prevention. Ballistic resistance training (BRT) involves high velocity and impact forces with lower loads. The Resistance Exercise Programme on Risk of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis in Females (REPROOF) study examined effects of BRT and CRT, relative to control (CON) on proximal femur BMD. Healthy postmenopausal women aged 50-70 years were randomised into BRT, CRT or CON groups. BRT and CRT conducted supervised resistance training twice weekly for eight months. In CRT, concentric and eccentric phases each lasted ~2 s at 55-80% of one-repetition maximum (1RM). BRT involved explosive (maximum velocity) concentric movements at 20-50% of 1RM. Proximal femur and lumbar spine BMD were measured by DXA; tibia structure by peripheral QCT. Groups were compared using ANCOVA, adjusting for baseline values. Of 109 women randomised, 82 (63.1 ± 3.7 years; 24.5 ± 3.5 kgm-2; femoral neck T-score -1.1 ± 0.8) completed the study, with 98% adherence. BRT improved total hip BMD (+0.008 [0.001, 0.014] g/cm2; P = 0.02) versus CON. CRT did not affect hip BMD but tibial shaft cortical BMD increased (+4.141 [1.007, 7.274] g/cm2; P = 0.01) and cortical thickness declined relative to CON (-0.07 [-0.13, -0.01] mm; P = 0.03), accompanied by tibial shaft widening. BRT increased total hip and trochanter BMD (P ≤ 0.03) in the subgroup with low BMD. BRT benefitted proximal femur BMD relative to CON, including in the subgroup with low BMD. CRT did not affect hip BMD but caused tibial shaft structural adaptation that may affect strength in bending. BRT based interventions should be further developed and evaluated for osteoporosis prevention.

title: Effects of Intermittent Hypoxia in Sprint Interval Training on Performance and Physiological Responses: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Ribeiro, Felipe Alves, Germano Marcolino Putti, Júlia Causin Andreossi, Carlos Dellavechia de Carvalho, and Marcelo Papoti. Effects of intermittent hypoxia in sprint interval training on performance and physiological responses: a systematic review. High Alt Med Biol. 00:00-00, 2026.
OBJECTIVE: To synthesize the acute and chronic effects of sprint interval training (SIT) in hypoxia (SIH) on performance and physiological responses.
METHODS: This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Seven databases were searched from inception to August 14, 2025. Eligible studies compared hypoxic and normoxic conditions during acute or chronic SIT protocols comprising at least three repeated all-out efforts of 30 seconds interspersed by ∼4.5 minutes in healthy physically active or trained adults. Study selection, risk-of-bias assessment, and data extraction were conducted independently by two reviewers.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies were included, comprising 11 acute crossover studies and 7 chronic parallel-group studies. Seventeen studies used cycling and one tethered swimming. Acutely, peak power was generally preserved, whereas mean power and total work were more frequently impaired during severe or continuous hypoxia. Hypoxia often reduced peripheral oxygen saturation, oxygen uptake, peak oxygen uptake, muscle oxygen saturation, and oxyhemoglobin during exercise. Chronic SIT improved aerobic and performance outcomes, including oxygen uptake, time to exhaustion, time-trial performance, and critical power; however, SIH was not consistently superior to normoxic SIT.
CONCLUSIONS: SIH provides a substantial acute systemic and peripheral hypoxic stimulus, but its additional performance benefit remains inconsistent and appears to depend on hypoxic severity, hypoxic dose, recovery structure, and training status.

title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intense exercise may transiently alter iron metabolism through inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms. Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) may influence these responses and short-term iron regulation. This study evaluated the effects of black chokeberry supplementation on iron metabolism, inflammation, antioxidant capacity, and hematological status in female competitive swimmers.
METHODS: Twenty-two female swimmers (13.14 ± 1.42 years) were randomly allocated to a supplementation or placebo group. Participants completed two identical swimming tests comprising 800-, 200-, and 50-m efforts before and after 57.32 ± 8.31 days of supplementation. Blood was collected before exercise, immediately after exercise, and after 3 h of recovery.
RESULTS: Most inflammatory markers showed time-dependent changes without significant group effects. C-reactive protein decreased from pre- to post-exercise during the second test in the supplemented group (p = 0.0325; Cohen's d = 1.29), whereas placebo recovery values increased between tests (p < 0.0001; Cohen's d = 3.33). Total antioxidant capacity showed a significant time × group interaction (p = 0.0007), with higher recovery values in the supplemented group. Iron, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and total iron-binding capacity showed significant time effects (all p < 0.0001). Hepcidin also showed a significant time effect, with significant within-group increases only in the placebo group. Transferrin was lower in the supplemented group at Post II (p = 0.0071; Cohen's d = 1.17), whereas ferritin remained unchanged and hematological parameters showed no consistent between-group differences.
CONCLUSION: Black chokeberry supplementation may influence markers related to short-term post-exercise iron availability, potentially in association with inflammatory and antioxidant responses, without detectable effects on body iron stores or erythropoiesis.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT06486623; registration date: 2024-07-03).

title: Recovery Kinetics After Particulated Autologous Cartilage With Platelet-Rich Plasma for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus in Athletes: Functional Scores Track Function but Show Limited Return-to-Sport Prediction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Talar cartilage repair is reported through 12-month endpoints; first-year recovery, a 6-month assessment's predictive value, and sex differences remain unknown.
PURPOSE: To characterize recovery after PACI-PRP for talar osteochondral lesions in athletes and whether 6-month scores predict 12-month function and return to sport (RTS).
METHODS: A secondary analysis of a prospective registry included 50 athletes with talar-dome lesions. FADI (primary), VAS pain, and Karlsson-Petersson scores at baseline, 6, and 12 months were analyzed with the Friedman test and mixed-effects models with a time-by-sex interaction. Front-loading (the share of the 12-month change reached by 6 months), correlation with 12-month scores, and the ROC-curve area (AUC) for RTS were computed.
RESULTS: All outcomes improved (p < 0.001). Recovery was front-loaded, with 67% (FADI), 71% (VAS), and 75% (Karlsson) of the 12-month gain by 6 months. Six-month scores correlated moderately with 12-month function (r = 0.44 to 0.58) but did not usefully discriminate RTS (AUC, 0.41 to 0.61). Early responders (MCID by 6 months) had a higher but non-significant RTS rate than late responders (20/21 vs 21/28; p = 0.115), with comparable 12-month function (86 vs 83; p = 0.242). No significant sex differences were identified (interaction p = 0.234 and 0.070).
CONCLUSIONS: Recovery after PACI-PRP is front-loaded with no significant sex differences. Six-month scores forecast 1-year function moderately and did not usefully predict RTS, indicating that return to play depends on factors beyond joint-specific function - psychological readiness and sport-specific load - warranting prospective study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic study, Level IV.

title: Normative Thresholds for Upper Extremity Functional Testing in Adolescent Athletes: Outcome Measures of Strength.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The use of functional upper extremity measures to guide rehabilitation, reduce injury risk, and inform return-to-play decision-making has increased. However, assessment of these measures has focused primarily on collegiate and adult athletes.
HYPOTHESIS: Normative thresholds would differ by dominance, with stronger values exhibited on the dominant limb.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross sectional.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.
METHODS: Healthy, adolescent athletes who reported participation in either contact or overhead upper-extremity sports completed an upper extremity functional test battery administered in a randomized order. Strength measures of internal rotation (IR) and external rotation (ER) as well as the athletic shoulder (ASH) test were collected in prone using a handheld dynamometer. Descriptive statistics were calculated for all outcome measures with separate analyses for dominant (DOM) and nondominant (NON) limbs. The 15th percentile was computed and used to establish performance thresholds. Strength measures were compared between limbs using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with effect sizes calculated. Descriptive statistics were computed to compare exploratorily male versus female and sport-based performance for all strength measures.
RESULTS: A total of 156 participants (78.2% male; 60.2% contact athletes; age, 16.5 ± 1.2 years; weight, 162.8 ± 39.2 lbs) were included for analysis. Norms and percentile thresholds across tests are presented, with shoulder strength thresholds consistently greater in the DOM limb. DOM IR strength was significantly greater than NON IR strength (P = 0.002). ASH performance was greater in the DOM limb for the I position (180 degrees of shoulder abduction; P < 0.001) and Y position (135 degrees of abduction; P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Performance in healthy, adolescent athletes is influenced by limb dominance and task-specificity and indicates that reliance on collegiate or adult-derived normative values may not be appropriate.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These normative thresholds provide a clinically meaningful framework to guide rehabilitation progression and evidence-based decision-making and will serve as the foundation for future work establishing whether these measures are associated with or predictive of subsequent injury.

title: Targeting Medial Leg Pain in Athletes: Distinguishing Between Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome and Tibialis Posterior Tendinopathy.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To examine the clinical overlap between medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS) and tibialis posterior tendinopathy (TPT) in athletes with exercise-induced medial lower leg pain. Current evidence regarding anatomy, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, imaging, and management is reviewed to improve diagnostic accuracy and highlight emerging concepts regarding posterior tibial tendon (PTT) involvement in athletes traditionally diagnosed with "shin splints."
RECENT FINDINGS: Although MTSS remains the most common diagnosis for exercise-induced medial tibial pain, growing biomechanical and imaging evidence suggests PTT pathology may be more prevalent than previously recognized, particularly in athletic populations. MTSS and TPT share overlapping symptom location, gradual onset, and activity-related pain, contributing to potential misdiagnosis. Despite these similarities, important distinctions exist in physical examination findings, foot biomechanics, imaging characteristics, and treatment strategies. Additionally, evolving concepts surrounding progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD) have better defined the relationship between PTT pathology and medial foot and ankle instability. The broad clinical diagnosis of "shin splints" may encompass a subset of athletes with unrecognized TPT. Careful assessment of PTT function, foot alignment, and lower extremity biomechanics should complement evaluation of medial lower leg pain athletes. Improved recognition of TPT may facilitate earlier diagnosis, guide appropriate rehabilitation, prevent progression to PCFD, and identify opportunities for future prospective studies directly comparing MTSS and TPT in athletic populations.

title: Risk, Knowledge, and Awareness of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) in Elite Female Volleyball Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a condition caused by low energy availability (LEA) and is associated with adverse health and performance outcomes in athletes. Although volleyball involves considerable physical stress and repetitive jumping, little is known about RED-S knowledge and risk of LEA in elite female volleyball players.
HYPOTHESIS: Elite female volleyball athletes have limited awareness of RED-S, and athletes at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q are more likely to be injured.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Elite female volleyball athletes competing in the Turkish Women's Elite Volleyball League during the 2024-2025 season were recruited. Participants completed an online survey including demographic information, the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), and items assessing knowledge, awareness, and support-seeking behaviors related to RED-S. Athletes were classified as "at risk" for LEA using a LEAF-Q cutoff score of ≥8. Associations between LEAF-Q risk status and injury history during the previous year were analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 148 athletes participated. The mean LEAF-Q score was 5.50 ± 3.48, and 25% of athletes were classified as at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q. Most athletes (92.6%) reported never having heard of RED-S or the Female Athlete Triad. Athletes identified as at risk by the LEAF-Q were significantly more likely to have sustained an injury in the previous year than athletes not at risk (odds ratio, 7.86; 95% CI, 3.03-20.41).
CONCLUSION: Elite female volleyball athletes demonstrated low knowledge of RED-S, while a substantial proportion were identified as at risk for LEA. LEA risk was associated strongly with injury history, supporting the clinical relevance of LEAF-Q screening in this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine LEAF-Q screening combined with sport-specific education may facilitate early identification of athletes who may require further clinical evaluation for LEA-related problems and may inform prevention-oriented support strategies in elite female volleyball players.

title: Bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps tendon autografts are associated with a higher 1-year risk of thigh muscle injury after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in competitive male athletes: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the association between anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) graft type and subsequent thigh muscle injury in athletes involved in pivoting sports.
METHODS: A retrospective observational study was conducted on 221 ACLRs performed in 199 competitive male athletes involved in pivoting sports, classified according to graft donor site: extensor mechanism (bone-patellar tendon-bone [BPTB] or quadriceps tendon) and flexor mechanism (hamstring tendon). Only athletes who returned to sport and completed a minimum of 12 months of follow-up were included. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed thigh muscle injuries occurring within the first year following the discharge date were identified and classified by muscle group injured and graft type.
RESULTS: Thirty-five athletes (15.8%) sustained at least one MRI-confirmed thigh muscle injury (41 muscle-group-level injuries in total) in the year after discharge from ACLR. Athletes who received a graft from the extensor mechanism had a higher proportion of any thigh muscle injury than those with hamstring grafts (27/133, 20.3% vs. 8/88, 9.1%; absolute risk difference 11.2%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.4-20.0; odds ratio [OR] 2.45, 95% CI 1.12-5.88; p = 0.037). Muscle-group analyses showed no significant differences for hamstring injury or quadriceps injury. All six adductor injuries occurred in the extensor donor group (4.5% vs. 0%), but this difference was not statistically robust. After adjustment, none of the three muscle-group comparisons remained significant.
CONCLUSION: Extensor mechanism grafts were associated with a higher proportion of athletes sustaining any thigh muscle injury in the year following discharge from rehabilitation; although absolute rates were low, no individual muscle group showed a significant difference.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Arthroscopy-Assisted Lower Trapezius Tendon Transfer Provides Superior Midterm Outcomes and Return to Work/Sport Compared With Latissimus Dorsi Tendon Transfer for Irreparable Posterosuperior Rotator Cuff Tears.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare midterm return to work (RTW) and return to sport (RTS) rates, clinical outcomes, muscle strength, and radiologic survivorship between arthroscopy-assisted lower trapezius tendon transfer (aLTT) and arthroscopy-assisted latissimus dorsi tendon transfer (aLDT) in patients with posterosuperior irreparable rotator cuff tears.
METHODS: This retrospective comparative study included patients who underwent aLDT or aLTT for posterosuperior irreparable rotator cuff tears between January 2012 and October 2020, with a minimum follow-up of 5 years. The primary outcomes were RTW and RTS rates. Secondary clinical outcomes included patient-reported outcome measures, active range of motion, and active range of motion strength. Radiological outcomes included acromiohumeral distance and Hamada grade. Graft integrity was assessed using postoperative magnetic resonance imaging. Factors associated with RTW and RTS were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 94 patients were divided into 2 groups according to the surgical procedure: the aLDT group (n = 44) underwent aLDT, and the aLTT group (n = 50) underwent aLTT. The aLTT group showed significantly higher RTW (90.0% vs 72.7%, P = .035) and RTS (88.6% vs 63.3%, P = .020) rates than the aLDT group. Both groups showed significant postoperative improvements in clinical outcomes. Postoperative Constant scores (50.7 ± 11.0 vs 64.8 ± 12.8, P < .001), American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons scores (70.5 ± 10.8 vs 83.8 ± 11.8, P < .001), Activities of Daily Living requiring External Rotation scores (20.6 ± 5.7 vs 25.7 ± 3.9, P < .001), forward elevation (135.7° ± 31.7° vs 153.3° ± 22.5°, P = .005), external rotation at the side (34.1° ± 9.5° vs 54.4° ± 22.9°, P < .001), forward elevation strength (20.4 ± 4.2 N vs 24.5 ± 4.4 N, P < .001), and external rotation strength (19.3 ± 3.7 N vs 23.9 ± 4.8 N, P < .001) were all significantly higher in the aLTT group compared with the aLDT group. The progression of arthritic changes was significantly greater in the aLDT group (50%) compared with the aLTT group (12%) (P < .001). Postoperative forward elevation strength, external rotation strength, and progression of arthritic changes were independently associated with higher odds of RTW and RTS.
CONCLUSIONS: aLTT showed superior RTW and RTS outcomes compared with aLDT at midterm follow-up. These functional advantages were accompanied by greater clinical improvements and more favorable radiologic parameters, reflecting the biomechanical superiority of the aLTT.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Lower extremity joint biomechanics from a single crossover drop task demonstrate superior predictive potential for secondary ACL injuries than drop vertical jump or single leg landing tasks.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Secondary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries remain a significant concern after return-to-sport (RTS) following ACL reconstruction (ACLR), with rates as high as 24%. Identifying biomechanical predictors of re-injury is critical for improving RTS protocols.
PURPOSE: To compare the predictive potential of three common landing tasks [drop vertical jump (DVJ), single-leg landing (SLL), and single-leg crossover drop (SCD)] for secondary ACL injury risk in post-ACLR athletes.
METHODS: A multicenter cohort of 150 athletes (age 13-30 years) that were cleared for RTS post-ACLR completed DVJ, SLL, and SCD tasks during 3D motion analysis; 144 athletes data met criteria for analysis. Peak kinematic and kinetic variables (n = 126) were analyzed using a penalized logistic regression with an elastic net penalty. Predictive models were evaluated via ROC curves, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values.
RESULTS: The SCD task demonstrated the strongest predictive performance for secondary ACL injury, with a validated positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.57, negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.96, sensitivity of 80.0%, specificity of 88.9%, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.933. The DVJ demonstrated moderate predictive performance (PPV=0.43, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=85.7%, AUC=0.843), while the SLL demonstrated the lowest performance (PPV=0.33, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=78.6%, AUC=0.736).
CONCLUSION: Lower extremity biomechanics during SCD provide greater predictive performance for secondary ACL injury compared with the DVJ or SLL. The findings suggest that SCD captures biomechanical characteristics relevant to secondary ACL injury risk and may improve identification of athletes at elevated risk following ACL reconstruction. However, further validation and model simplification are needed before clinical implementation as a stand-alone screening tool.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Does Smoking Impair Functional Recovery After Total Knee Arthroplasty? A Large-Scale Analysis of Patient-Reported Outcomes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Smoking is a recognized risk factor that adversely affects wound healing, systemic health, and orthopedic outcomes. However, its influence on patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) after total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains insufficiently defined. This study evaluated the association between smoking and postoperative PROMs following primary TKA.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 992 patients who underwent primary TKA between January 2020 and January 2023 was analyzed. Patients were categorized as smokers (n = 152, 15.3%) or nonsmokers (n = 840, 84.7%). PROMs included the EQ-5D-5L index, EQ-VAS, and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) subscales assessing pain, symptoms, activities of daily living, sports/recreation, and quality of life. Outcomes were recorded preoperatively and at 12 months postoperatively. Between-group comparisons were performed using independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests. Multivariate linear regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and baseline PROM scores.
RESULTS: Preoperative PROMs were comparable between smokers and nonsmokers (all p > 0.05). At 12 months, both groups demonstrated significant improvement compared with baseline (all p < 0.001). However, nonsmokers achieved higher postoperative scores than smokers, including EQ-5D-5L (0.82 ± 0.11 vs. 0.75 ± 0.13), EQ-VAS (75.6 ± 14.0 vs. 68.1 ± 15.5), and KOOS quality of life (67.9 ± 15.3 vs. 60.1 ± 16.8) (all p < 0.001). Improvements were also greater among nonsmokers (ΔEQ-VAS p < 0.001). Multivariate analysis confirmed smoking as an independent predictor of worse postoperative PROMs.
CONCLUSIONS: Smoking is an independent risk factor for poorer functional recovery and lower quality of life following primary TKA. These findings may be useful for preoperative patient counseling, indicating that smokers may experience not only an increased risk of postoperative complications, as established in previous studies, but also poorer patient-reported functional outcomes.

title: Lateral Femoral Condyle Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation Location for Osteochondral Defects of the Knee Is Associated With Selected Patient-Reported Outcome Differences but Not With Graft Reoperation or Failure.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), clinically significant outcome achievement, reoperation, and graft failure after isolated medial femoral condyle (MFC) and lateral femoral condyle (LFC) osteochondral allograft (OCA) transplantation.
METHODS: Consecutive patients who underwent OCA at a single cartilage restoration center from 2003 to 2023 were reviewed. Patients were included if they underwent isolated MFC or LFC OCA transplantation and had preoperative and minimum 2-year postoperative PROMs. When multiple postoperative PROMs were available, the most recent score at or beyond 2 years was used. Cohort-specific minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds were calculated as one-half the standard deviation of the change score. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models were adjusted for graft location, baseline PROM score, follow-up time, age, sex, Workers' Compensation status, athlete status, and laterality. Time to reoperation was compared with Kaplan-Meier/log-rank analysis and Cox regression.
RESULTS: A total of 141 patients were included (MFC: n = 79; LFC: n = 62). Follow-up data were available for 115 patients and averaged 6.2 ± 3.0 years (range, 2.0-16.3 years), with no difference between MFC and LFC cohorts (6.2 ± 2.9 vs 6.2 ± 3.2 years; P = .963). In adjusted linear models accounting for baseline PROM score, follow-up time, age, sex, Workers' Compensation status, athlete status, laterality, and ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation status, the LFC recipient site was associated with higher Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) Pain (β = 9.1; 95% confidence interval, 1.2-16.9; P = .024) and KOOS Quality of Life (QoL) (β = 12.3; 95% confidence interval, 1.6-23.0; P = .025) scores. After the same adjustment, the LFC recipient site was associated with greater odds of achieving cohort-specific MCID for KOOS QoL, whereas the corresponding KOOS Pain MCID association was attenuated to nonsignificance (P = .054) once ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation was included in the model; other threshold analyses were not significantly different. Reoperation rates were 27.8% for MFC and 29.0% for LFC (log-rank P = .805). Graft failure was rare (MFC, 2.5%; LFC, 0%; P = .504).
CONCLUSIONS: At a minimum 2-year follow-up, the LFC OCA recipient site was associated with higher adjusted KOOS Pain and KOOS QoL scores and higher adjusted odds of achieving cohort-specific MCID for KOOS QoL, an association that persisted after adjusting for ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation status. Graft location was not associated with reoperation or graft failure.

title: The role of visual and vestibular disturbances in predicting four-week recovery following acute concussion: a cohort study by sex (from the Toronto concussion study).
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Visual and vestibular disturbances (VVD) are common following concussion, but their relationship with recovery and potential sex differences remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the relationship between early VVD and four-week recovery overall and by sex in community-dwelling adults.
METHODS: This prospective longitudinal study included 122 adults (mean age 36.6 years; 64.6% female) assessed within one week and again four weeks post-concussion. VVD were assessed using the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool-5th Edition (SCAT-5) and a modified Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screen (mVOMS). Recovery was determined by physician evaluation. Logistic regression examined associations between early VVD and recovery while adjusting for injury and sociodemographic covariates.
RESULTS: Male and female participants demonstrated different baseline VVD patterns on the SCAT-5 and mVOMS. At four weeks, 27.9% had recovered. Baseline SCAT-5 visual and vestibular symptoms were not associated with recovery, whereas mVOMS positivity (symptom increase ≥ 4) was associated with non-recovery. No significant sex differences were observed in the association between early VVD and recovery.
CONCLUSIONS: Early mVOMS positivity may have prognostic value for identifying community-dwelling adults at risk of delayed concussion recovery, whereas self-reported visual and vestibular symptoms alone may not. Although early symptom profiles differed by sex, recovery trajectories did not.

title: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are more frequent in female football players, but sex-specific differences in injury characteristics remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to analyse sex-specific differences in ACL injury incidence and characteristics in professional football.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study used data from a German national ACL registry ('Kreuzbandregister im Deutschen Fußball'), including professional male (first to third league) and female (first and second league) football players from the 2016/2017 to 2024/2025 seasons. Incidence rates were compared using Poisson regression (incidence rate ratio, IRR) and injury characteristics using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: A total of 459 ACL injuries were analysed (177 female and 282 male). The rate was 1.19 versus 0.69 per 1000 match hours (IRR 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.13). The difference was most pronounced in the first division (IRR 2.49, 1.82-3.41) and smaller and not significant in the lower leagues (IRR 1.24, 0.93-1.65). Injuries in female players were more often non-contact (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.37) and indirect-contact injuries (aOR 2.92), occurred more often on artificial turf (aOR 5.42) and in national team players (aOR 3.03). Concomitant injury patterns did not differ significantly, except for fewer lateral collateral ligament injuries in women.
CONCLUSION: ACL injury rates are higher in female professional football players, particularly in the first division. The predominance of non-contact and indirect-contact mechanisms supports targeted, sex-specific prevention strategies.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

title: Return to play rate and performance after ulnar collateral ligament repair with suture tape augmentation in major league baseball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) repair with suture tape augmentation has emerged as an alternative to traditional reconstruction in appropriately selected patients. While clinical outcomes of UCL repair have been reported in amateur athletes, data evaluating performance outcomes in Major League Baseball (MLB) players remain limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate return to play (RTP) and changes in performance metrics among MLB players undergoing UCL repair with suture tape augmentation. We hypothesized that UCL repair would allow a faster RTP compared with historical reconstruction data while maintaining player performance.
METHODS: MLB players who underwent UCL repair with suture tape augmentation between 2016 and 2024 were identified using publicly available injury databases. Player performance metrics were obtained from publicly available databases including MLB Statcast. The primary outcome was time to RTP. Secondary outcomes included traditional and advanced performance metrics. For pitchers, metrics included earned run average, innings pitched, strikeouts, walk rate, fastball velocity, fastball spin rate, fielder independent pitching, fangraphs wins above replacement (fWAR), and Statcast-based metrics. Position player metrics included fWAR, fielding run value, and arm strength. Pre-operative and post-operative metrics were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests or Mann-Whitney tests with statistical significance set at P < .05.
RESULTS: Twenty-two MLB players met inclusion criteria. RTP to the MLB level was 81.8% (18/22). The mean RTP time was 10.98 months (range, 5.9-34). Pitchers had a mean RTP of 13.51 months (range, 9-34) and position players had a mean RTP of 7.51 months (range, 5.9-8.5). There were no statistically significant differences between pre-operative and post-operative performance metrics, including earned run average (3.66 ± 0.7 vs. 3.95 ± 1.9; P = .765), fastball velocity (93.0 ± 1.7 vs. 92.7 ± 1.9 mph; P = .609), innings pitched (42.1 ± 39.0 vs. 23.0 ± 28.0; P = .266), strikeouts (31.7 ± 53.7 vs. 23.5 ± 27.4; P = .247), or fastball spin rate (2,241 ± 131 vs. 2,235 ± 122 rpm; P = .496). Similarly, position players demonstrated no significant differences in fWAR, fielding run value, or arm strength after RTP.
CONCLUSION: UCL repair with suture tape augmentation in MLB players demonstrates a high rate of RTP with preservation of traditional and advanced performance metrics. Position players returned earlier than pitchers; overall RTP remained favorable. UCL repair with suture tape augmentation provides an effective surgical option allowing return to elite-level performance.

title: Survey Findings From Orthopaedic Surgeons in Asia-Pacific: Attitudes and Practice Patterns in Pediatric Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate current anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction rehabilitation recommendations among Asia-Pacific orthopaedic surgeons and compare them with previously published North American data.
METHODS: An online survey was conducted between January 2024 and June 2025, distributed to all orthopaedic surgeons within Pediatric Research in Sports Medicine Asia-Pacific in 2024, capturing clinical practice patterns at 3 key milestones: initiation of jogging, progression to modified sports activity, and unrestricted return to sport. Only orthopaedic surgeons within Pediatric Research in Sports Medicine Asia-Pacific who had provided informed consent to participate were included. The results were compared with a previously published survey of North American surgeons.
RESULTS: The survey was sent to 127 surgeons, and 54 (43%) responded. Agreement was greatest for jogging-80% recommending initiation at 3 to 4 months postoperatively. Consensus declined for later phases: modified sports activity between 4 and 8 months, whereas return to sport spanned from 6 to 12 months. Compared with Pediatric Research in Sports Medicine North America, where 92% allowed jogging at 3 to 4 months and return to sport often advised at 6 to 9 months, Asia-Pacific surgeons showed a delayed approach. Asia-Pacific respondents considered quadriceps and hamstring strength essential for progression, although modalities varied-manual muscle testing (60%) predominated over isokinetic (28%) or isometric (12%) methods. Functional testing was employed by 68% prior to modified sports activity, with variability in test type and criteria. Compared with North American peers, Asia-Pacific surgeons used more objective strength and functional assessments, with limited use of patient-reported outcomes (20%). At the time of return to sport, 73% recommended injury-prevention programs and 50% endorsed functional bracing, rates comparable to North America.
CONCLUSIONS: Acknowledging the temporal differences between both surveys and the evolution of rehabilitation practices during this period, the present study suggests a tendency toward conservative rehabilitation timelines in the Asia-Pacific region, with respect to return to jogging, return to modified sporting activity, and unrestricted return to sport. Strength and functional assessments are valued highly across both surveys, although differences exist in specific testing modalities employed and criteria used to guide progression.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This survey-based comparison provides insight into regional variation and temporal trends in surgeon-reported anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction rehabilitation practices. The findings may assist clinicians and researchers in contextualizing contemporary rehabilitation recommendations and highlight areas of variability that warrant further standardization.

title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized.
METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions.
RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.

title: Ramp lesions repaired during anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction are associated with similar functional outcomes to other medial meniscal lesions at 1 year: A prospective registry-based study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate 12-month outcomes after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) in patients with repaired ramp lesions compared with patients with other medial meniscal lesions or no meniscal lesions.
METHODS: This prospective registry-based study included patients undergoing primary ACLR with 12-month follow-up. Three propensity-score-matched comparisons were performed: ramp versus other medial meniscal lesions (94 vs. 94), ramp versus no meniscal lesions (107 vs. 205), and other medial meniscal lesions versus no meniscal lesions (103 vs. 103). Outcomes included knee function, psychological readiness, satisfaction and return to sport and work. Patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) and minimal clinically important difference (MCID) were defined as International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores ≥75.9 and improvements ≥10.7 points, respectively.
RESULTS: Among 110 patients with ramp lesions (60.9% male; mean age, 25.9 ± 8.9 years), knee function improved significantly at 12 months (p < 0.001). Postoperative IKDC scores did not differ significantly between ramp lesions and other medial meniscal lesions (86.6 vs. 84.5; p = 0.83) or no meniscal lesions (86.6 vs. 87.6; p = 0.15). However, compared with patients without meniscal lesions, those with ramp lesions reported lower subjective knee values (85.0 vs. 90.0; p = 0.007), psychological readiness (67.0 vs. 76.5; p = 0.02) and satisfaction (77.6% vs. 89.3%; p = 0.009). No significant differences were observed between other medial meniscal lesions and no meniscal lesions.
CONCLUSIONS: Repaired ramp lesions were associated with comparable functional outcomes but lower psychological readiness and satisfaction compared with isolated ACLR at 12 months, emphasizing the importance of patient-perceived recovery.

title: Heart rate variability in police research: a scoping review of objective psychophysiological assessment.
abstract: Policing places substantial psychological and physiological demands on officers, increasing the risk of adverse health outcomes and impaired performance. As wearable physiological sensing technologies have become more accessible, heart rate variability (HRV) has emerged as a widely used measure of autonomic and psychophysiological regulation. This scoping review synthesized the application of HRV in policing research and identified methodological considerations and future directions. PubMed, Web of Science, MEDLINE, and PsycINFO were systematically searched for primary studies involving police personnel that used HRV as a measure or outcome. Following screening and full-text review, 58 studies comprising 4,764 participants were included. A narrative synthesis identified three broad applications of HRV: (1) health and well-being, (2) stress response and performance, and (3) adaptive regulation. Lower HRV was consistently associated with occupational stress, shift work, poorer recovery, obesity, and metabolic dysfunction, whereas greater physical activity, aerobic fitness, and healthier body composition were associated with more adaptive autonomic profiles facilitating recovery from stress. During acute operational demands, reductions in vagally mediated HRV and greater sympathetic activation were generally associated with poorer performance, while broader HRV measures were linked to fatigue, tactical selection, and operational readiness. Breathing-based interventions, such as HRV biofeedback and mindfulness were associated with improvements in autonomic regulation, recovery, training adaptation, and performance. Despite these encouraging findings, substantial conceptual and methodological heterogeneity limited interpretation of the evidence. As a scoping review, the objective was to characterize the breadth of HRV applications in policing rather than estimate pooled effects. Accordingly, studies were included across diverse designs and HRV applications. HRV was used as an indicator of stress, recovery, autonomic regulation, health, and performance, with marked variation in theoretical frameworks, HRV metrics, sensing technologies, recording protocols, and outcome measures. Collectively, the findings demonstrate that HRV is a feasible objective measure in policing research. Future work should prioritize theory-driven study designs, standardized measurement, reporting, and methodological controls to strengthen objective inference from physiological sensing. Currently, HRV should be interpreted as one component of a broader psychophysiological assessment. It should not be used for personnel selection, fitness-for-duty, or prediction of mental health.

title: Thumb muscle activation with task-specific exercise: A pilot study with participant self-report implementation outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis is a common source of pain, weakness, and reduced hand function and upper extremity rehabilitation. Although isometric stabilization exercises are commonly used in hand therapy to support dynamic thumb carpometacarpal control, limited task-specific evidence guides exercise selection.
PURPOSE: To examine muscle activation across four isometric thumb-hand positions in healthy adults and describe participant perceptions of the protocol's acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness before testing in symptomatic hand therapy samples.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional, within-subject repeated-measures pilot study.
METHODS: Seven healthy right-handed adults (mean age, 22.7 ± 0.48 years) performed four submaximal isometric exercise conditions at approximately 80% perceived effort: composite finger-thumb squeeze, "bunny-ears" pinch, resisted index-finger abduction, and fingertip-only press. Surface electromyography was recorded from the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, first dorsal interosseous, and forearm flexor group. Integrated electromyography was normalized within participants to each muscle's maximum response across conditions. A two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (condition × muscle) compared normalized activation. Participants rated acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness on five-point Likert scales.
RESULTS: Normalized activation differed by muscle, F(3,18) = 14.22, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.70, with a significant condition × muscle interaction, F(9,54) = 7.29, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55. Abductor pollicis brevis activation was highest during composite squeeze and bunny-ears pinch (0.93 ± 0.05 and 0.85 ± 0.06) and lowest during resisted index-finger abduction (0.31 ± 0.07). Opponens pollicis activation was highest during composite squeeze and resisted index-finger abduction (0.79 ± 0.07 and 0.75 ± 0.09). Mean construct-based ratings of acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ranged from 4.54-4.79 out of 5.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings provide preliminary evidence to inform hand therapy exercise selection by showing that functional isometric thumb-hand positions produce distinct intrinsic and extrinsic activation profiles. Favorable participant perceptions support protocol refinement and testing in larger and symptomatic hand therapy samples.

title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Effects of neuromuscular electrical stimulation applied simultaneously with exercise therapy in patellofemoral pain: A single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simultaneous neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) during exercise may augment task-specific quadriceps activation, but its additional effects in patellofemoral pain (PFP) are uncertain. This pilot trial examined whether adding simultaneous NMES improved pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, quadriceps strength, and muscle thickness compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation.
METHODS: In this single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial, 30 participants were allocated 1:1 to an intervention group or acontrol group. Both groups received the same hip- and knee-targeted exercise therapy twice weekly for 6 weeks. The intervention group received NMES during leg press and leg extension exercises, whereas the control group wore the same device with stimulation intensity set to zero. The primary outcome was worst pain during the previous week, assessed using the visual analogue scale(VAS). Secondary outcomes included the anterior knee pain scale (AKPS), Y-Balance Test (YBT) composite score, isokinetic quadriceps strength (60°/s, 180°/s), and quadriceps muscle thickness.
RESULTS: No additional between-group benefit was detected for worst pain (p = .96; Cohen's d = -0.03), AKPS (p = .26; Cohen's d = -0.24), YBT composite (p = .28; Cohen's d = -0.26), isokinetic strength at 60°/s (p = .67; Cohen's d = -0.11), or 180°/s (p = .56; Cohen's d = -0.12). Total quadriceps muscle thickness increased more in the intervention group than in the control group, but the effect was small (p = .03; Cohen's d = -0.27). No adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSION: No additional short-term benefit of adding simultaneous NMES to exercise therapy was detected for pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, or quadriceps strength compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation. A small increase in total quadriceps muscle thickness was detected, but its clinical relevance remains uncertain. These findings do not support routine addition of simultaneous NMES for short-term pain relief or functional improvement.

title: Body recomposition in adults: mechanisms, modulators, and practical algorithms for simultaneous skeletal muscle mass gain and fat mass loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body recomposition is the concurrent increase in fat-free mass (FFM) or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass (FM) within the same intervention period. Although hypertrophy is commonly pursued in energy surplus and FM loss in energy deficit, controlled trials indicate that recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training (PRT), adequate protein intake, and an appropriate energy prescription are combined.
METHODS: We conducted a structured narrative review of randomised trials, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies in adults, with emphasis on FFM, FM, strength, and performance outcomes. Device heterogeneity was considered when interpreting evidence, with greatest weight placed on four-compartment and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcomes.
RESULTS: PRT combined with higher protein intake, typically ~1.6-2.4 g/kg/day and higher relative intakes during energy restriction or leanness, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition. Effects are largest in untrained individuals and those with higher adiposity, smaller in trained or lean athletes, and still feasible in older adults when anabolic resistance is addressed with supervised PRT and sufficient protein. Moderate deficits, carbohydrate allocation around key sessions, sleep, and recovery support FFM retention or accretion while facilitating FM loss. Practical applications: Programmes should pair progressive overload with protein-centred diets, modest energy deficits, and periodic monitoring of body composition and performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Body recomposition is feasible but context-dependent; expected changes are generally modest in trained or lean populations and require individualised adjustment.

title: Citrulline Malate Ingestion Enhances Muscular Performance During a Selected Hypertrophy Hack Squat Training Protocol.
abstract: Wax, B, Dorgo, S, Montalvo, S, Lyons, B, and Mayo, JJ. Citrulline malate ingestion enhances muscular performance during a selected hypertrophy hack squat training protocol. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined potential ergogenic effects of an oral citrulline malate supplement (CM) during lower-body resistance training. Fifteen resistance-trained men completed a randomized, counterbalanced, double-blind crossover design. Subjects ingested 8.0 g CM or placebo 60 minutes before 8 sets of hack squats at 67% one-repetition maximum to failure with 90-second recovery intervals, repeating the protocol with the alternate treatment 1 week later. Blood lactate before and after exercise, rating of perceived exertion after sets 4 and 8, muscle soreness at 24 and 48 hours, and heart rate and blood pressure at rest and 5 and 10 minutes after exercise were assessed. Hack squat repetition numbers were higher overall in the CM condition (condition effect p = 0.0213), and CM increased total repetitions by 10.7 (95% confidence interval 1.4 to 20.0; p = 0.0265; Hedges' g = 0.61) and total workload by 1,064.7 units (95% confidence interval 84.1 to 2045.4; p = 0.0354; Hedges' g = 0.57). Blood lactate increased after exercise but did not differ by condition. Rating of perceived exertion showed no significant condition effect or Holm-adjusted set-specific difference. Citrulline malate was associated with significantly lower muscle soreness overall and at both 24 and 48 hours after exercise. Heart rate and systolic blood pressure showed condition × time interactions, with Holm-adjusted CM vs. placebo differences at 5 minutes after exercise, whereas diastolic blood pressure showed no significant condition effect or Holm-adjusted time-point difference. Acute CM supplementation may improve lower-body resistance training work capacity and reduce perceived soreness without altering lactate accumulation or perceived exertion.

title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition and quadriceps activation failure after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: Early assessment and rehabilitation beyond strength.
abstract: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) is common in the early postoperative period after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and can persist throughout rehabilitation. However, clinically assessing AMI is challenging, typically requiring muscle stimulation-based testing with dynamometry and/or electromyography (EMG) to estimate the precise degree of quadriceps activation failure. However, a reliable clinical examination can identify and grade the overt contraction impairment, extension loss and hamstring contracture often associated with laboratory assayed AMI. A recent report found 49% of patients at 3 weeks and 24% at 6 weeks after ACLR present with at least one clinically detectable sign of likely AMI. Preoperative clinical AMI, greater immediate postoperative pain and absence of preoperative physiotherapy were associated with higher prevalence of clinical AMI at 3 weeks, highlighting the vital nature of early physiotherapy and pain management. As the patient progresses, since AMI refers to the neural inhibition of the muscle secondary to joint injury, strength gains can actually coexist with persistent activation deficits. Thus, traditional strengthening programs may not be achieving optimal efficiency when attempting to restore strength after joint injury. Rehabilitation that integrates activation exercises, symptom management and progressive strengthening, with neuromuscular electrical stimulation and/or biofeedback may reduce AMI and enhance recovery. At return to sport, strength recovery should not be interpreted as proof of activation recovery and specialised muscle activation testing should be considered selectively when clinical testing is inconclusive. Future studies should determine whether identifying and treating activation deficits improves functional recovery and informs safer return-to-sport decisions.

title: Global Perspective in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Soccer Players: Current Concepts for the 2026 World Cup.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in soccer players represent a major challenge in modern sports medicine, particularly among elite athletes. Despite significant advances in surgical techniques, graft biology, and rehabilitation protocols graft failure rates, reinjury, and suboptimal return-to-sport outcomes remain clinically relevant concerns. Contemporary approaches emphasize a multifactorial strategy encompassing injury prevention, individualized graft selection, restoration of rotational and multiplanar stability, meniscal preservation, and criteria-based return-to-sport progression. Data from global registries and patient groups show that graft failure rates approach 10% for all types of grafts. This highlights the importance of a more holistic surgical approach that addresses the entire knee rather than focusing solely on replacing individual ligaments. There is growing evidence that adding lateral extra-articular procedures reduces failure rates, especially in high-risk athletes such as soccer players where cutting and pivoting are common. It is also crucial to recognize and treat concomitant injuries including meniscal tears, posterior meniscal root injuries, and medial instability to improve long-term outcomes. It is important to provide a comprehensive overview of anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in soccer players, integrating insights from an international symposium held in 2026 with the latest evidence available. Key areas covered include injury prevention strategies, biomechanics of injuries, graft selection, restoration of rotational stability, meniscal function preservation, rehabilitation approaches, and future directions for personalized medicine.

title: The knee replacement that never happened: a case of recovery following structured neuromuscular rehabilitation.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and reduced mobility, often leading patients to consider total knee replacement (TKR). Exercise is recommended as part of treatment; however, there is little guidance on the optimal type or duration of rehabilitation before surgery. As a result, some patients may be listed for TKR before receiving a structured trial of nonoperative care. We report the case of a 78-year-old woman with symptomatic knee OA placed on a National Health Service waiting list for TKR. While awaiting surgery, she undertook the Awareness, Resistance, Individualized, Stability, and Essential OrthoPrehab programme, a structured neuromuscular rehabilitation programme focusing on joint awareness, movement control, proprioception, and strengthening. After 3 months, she experienced improvements in pain, function, and confidence, reduced reliance on analgesics, and withdrew from the surgical waiting list. This case highlights the potential of structured rehabilitation to help some patients avoid surgery.

title: Imaging and diagnosis of overuse shoulder injuries in overhead athletes.
abstract: Shoulder overuse injuries are highly prevalent among athletes participating in overhead sports such as baseball, tennis, swimming, and volleyball, where repetitive high-velocity loading imposes unique biomechanical demands on the glenohumeral complex. These injuries span a broad spectrum, including rotator cuff tears, subacromial/subdeltoid impingement, superior labrum anterior-to-posterior (SLAP) lesions, long head of the biceps tendinopathy, glenohumeral instability, internal impingement, glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD), and Little League shoulder. Accurate diagnosis requires an understanding of sport-specific biomechanics, particularly the extreme forces generated during the late cocking and early acceleration phases of throwing, which produce characteristic injury patterns such as posterosuperior partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears and type II SLAP lesions via the peel-back mechanism. Imaging plays a central role in diagnosis and management. Radiographs remain the initial study for evaluating osseous anatomy and acromial morphology. MRI is the principal modality for soft-tissue assessment, while MR arthrography offers superior sensitivity for intra-articular pathology, including labral and partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears. Musculoskeletal ultrasound provides dynamic, cost-effective evaluation of tendons and bursae, and 3D CT or zero-time echo (ZTE) MRI is essential for quantifying glenoid bone loss in the setting of instability. Because many imaging findings are present in asymptomatic athletes, careful clinical correlation is essential. This review summarizes the imaging features, diagnostic pearls, and limitations of current modalities for shoulder overuse injuries in overhead athletes.

title: Ultrasound-guided needling release combined with platelet-rich plasma injection for refractory heel pain: A case report.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Refractory heel pain is a clinically challenging condition of multifactorial origin, often complicating both diagnosis and treatment. No standard therapy exists for refractory heel pain, and clinical experience is limited. We report the efficacy of ultrasound-guided needling release of calcific deposits combined with autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection and systematic rehabilitation in a patient with refractory heel pain.
PATIENT CONCERNS: A 57-year-old self-employed female patient presented with a 3-year history of recurrent redness, swelling, and pain in the right heel, with symptoms worsening after activity. In the month prior to admission, pain had progressively worsened, limiting her ability to stand, walk, and perform daily activities.
DIAGNOSES: Refractory right heel pain (chronic calcifying Achilles tendinitis, Achilles tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis with bone spur formation).
INTERVENTIONS: The procedure involved ultrasound-guided fenestration and disruption of calcifications at the Achilles tendon insertion, followed by intralesional PRP injection and a 6-month staged rehabilitation program.
OUTCOMES: At 1 week postoperatively, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) decreased to 3, and the patient could walk independently. At 1 month, VAS was 2, and she returned to work and daily activities. At 3 months, VAS was 1, American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society score improved to 90, and pain was largely resolved. The favorable outcome persisted at 6-month follow-up.
LESSONS: The combination of ultrasound-guided precise lesion management, PRP-based biological repair, and systematic rehabilitation offers a minimally invasive, safe, and effective strategy for refractory heel pain, serving as a valuable clinical reference for similar cases.

abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. It also examines diagnosis, treatment, and return to play considerations. Early recognition and appropriate management help ensure a safe and timely return to sport.

title: The Unique Features of Pediatric Sports Injuries: Shoulder Instability-Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Dislocations.
abstract: Traumatic anterior shoulder dislocations are common in youth athletes and occur more frequently in males and older adolescents. Dislocations typically result from direct trauma to the arm while in extension, abduction, and external rotation. Other risk factors include increased skeletal maturity and joint laxity. Inspection is a key component of the physical examination in the acute postdislocation setting, whereas provocative instability tests are useful for eliciting a history of dislocation. A standard two-view radiographic protocol is recommended for any patient with a first-time dislocation, and advanced imaging facilitates more reliable identification of concomitant bony and soft-tissue injuries such as Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions. Management is guided by age, structural abnormalities, likelihood of recurrence, and other patient-specific factors. Nonsurgical treatment features brief immobilization followed by progressive rehabilitation, whereas surgical treatment focuses on surgically repairing shoulder stabilizers. Despite high return-to-sport rates in the pediatric and adolescent population, the risk of recurrent dislocations is also high.

title: Return to sports after pediatric brain tumors: Time to move beyond survival.
abstract: Brain tumors are the second most common malignancy in children and adolescents and the leading cause of cancer-related death in this population. While survival rates have improved, survivors are at risk of neurocognitive, motor, and psychosocial sequelae due to both tumor location and treatments used. Participation in sport is increasingly recognized as beneficial for functional recovery, cardiorespiratory fitness, and overall well-being in children and adolescents treated for brain tumors. However, return to play (RTP) may pose some challenges, particularly in the presence of neurosurgical devices, cranial radiotherapy, or residual neurological deficits. This narrative clinical review summarizes current evidence on the risks of sport-related injuries in pediatric brain tumor patients and survivors, highlighting factors influencing vulnerability, including treatment history and specific sport characteristics. We propose a risk-based framework for RTP evaluation emphasizing individualized coordinated assessment by pediatric oncologists, neurosurgeons, and sports medicine specialists. Protective strategies are discussed, although evidence for concussion prevention remains limited. A safe RTP should be enhanced by the here-proposed structured evaluation, balancing safety with the physical, cognitive, and psychosocial benefits of active participation. This framework aims to support clinicians and families in facilitating safe and effective reintegration of pediatric brain tumor survivors into both recreational and competitive sports.

title: Bucket-Handle Meniscus Tears.
abstract: Bucket-handle meniscus tears represent a distinct and surgically significant pattern of meniscal injury, most commonly occurring in young, active patients and frequently associated with anterior cruciate ligament injury. The displaced central fragment produces a mechanical block to terminal knee extension, requiring prompt recognition and surgical intervention. Meniscal preservation through repair is the preferred approach when tissue quality and vascularity permit. It is important to review the diagnosis, surgical indications, repair techniques, and postoperative rehabilitation of bucket-handle meniscus tears, with a focus on evidence-based decision making for single-stage versus two-stage surgery, inside-out versus all-inside repair, adjunct techniques such as medial collateral ligament pie crusting and biologic augmentation, and criteria-based return to sport.

title: Orthobiologics 2026: State of the Art.
abstract: Orthobiologics are biologic products intended to promote healing and manage a range of musculoskeletal conditions. The field has evolved from a loosely defined collection of regenerative products into one that increasingly demands product-specific biology, indication-specific evidence, and disciplined postmarket surveillance. The strongest current clinical support remains for platelet-rich plasma for selected knee osteoarthritis and tendinopathy indications, whereas platelet-poor plasma may represent a distinct muscle-healing strategy. Cell-based therapies such as concentrated bone marrow aspirate and adipose-derived products remain biologically appealing but clinically heterogeneous, with outcomes influenced by harvest technique, processing method, route of administration, host phenotype, and disease severity. Perinatal tissue products, exosomes, and gene therapy occupy different positions on the translational spectrum: amniotic or placental products have the most mature clinical programs among emerging orthobiologic therapies, exosomes remain predominantly preclinical and highly regulated, and intra-articular gene transfer has now entered human trials with sustained transgene expression. A recurring theme across all presentations was that orthobiologics should no longer be studied as black-box interventions. Instead, progress will depend on linking clinical outcomes to rigorous product characterization, biomarker analysis, and scalable registry infrastructure. The Biologics Association Registry and Biorepository and the linked American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Orthobiologics Registry represent an important attempt to generate real-world evidence while simultaneously measuring the biologic content of what is injected. It is important to summarize the state of the art across blood-derived products, cell-based therapies, advanced acellular therapeutics, and registry science and outline the priorities that should guide orthopaedic practice and research over the next cycle of orthobiologic development.

title: Adhesive and Antibacterial Bio-Based Hydrogel for Human Voice Recognition and Osteoarthritis Recovery Monitoring.
abstract: Conductive hydrogels derived from natural polysaccharides hold great promise for next generation wearable electronics owing to their intrinsic biocompatibility, adhesiveness, and tunable mechanical properties. However, realizing amylum-based hydrogels with simultaneously high stretchability, sensitivity, strong adhesion and antibacterial performance remains a significant challenge. Herein, a multifunctional ionic hydrogel, marked as PAPC4 hydrogel, composed of polyacrylamide (PAAm), amylum and phenol-modified chitosan is developed via a one-pot synthesis strategy. The hydrogel exhibits exceptional stretchability (up to 1605%), short response time (16.1 ms), high optical transparency (96%), strong adhesion (43.2 kPa on PVC) and pronounced antibacterial activity. Cytotoxicity assays, live/dead staining, and subcutaneous implantation supported its biocompatibility under the tested conditions, while bacterial assays demonstrated activity against Escherichia coli. As a strain sensor, PAPC4 detected joint movements and throat vibrations during speech. It also recorded differences in knee movement among control, osteoarthritis, and treated osteoarthritis groups in rats. These results support the use of this chitosan-starch composite hydrogel in wearable motion sensing and rehabilitation monitoring.
